title: The Variational Ceiling: Why Neural MI Estimators Can't See Past Log N
summary: If you have ever put mutual information in a loss and let a neural network maximise it, you have taken a position on a mathematical object that is more delicate than it looks. The Donsker–Varadhan identity makes the idea look painless....
body:
If you have ever put mutual information in a loss and let a neural network maximise it, you have taken a position on a mathematical object that is more delicate than it looks. The Donsker–Varadhan identity makes the idea look painless. $D_{KL}(P\|Q)$ is a supremum of a quantity you can estimate from samples; a neural network parameterises the test function; the gradient flows; out comes mutual information. The estimator that first packaged this cleanly — MINE — appeared in 2018 and became a workhorse. Since then a short library of papers has shown that, in the regime that actually matters for representation learning, this family of estimators is not just noisy but fundamentally limited. The limits are not bugs that a better architecture fixes. They are consequences of sampling theory and of the shape of the objective, and they explain why InfoNCE caps out at $\log K$, why MINE's error bars look fine in toy experiments and absurd on real data, and why "we maximised mutual information" is, on its own, a weak claim.

## Why this matters now

Mutual information entered deep learning as a framing — the information bottleneck, deep infomax, contrastive predictive coding — and stayed as a loss. Contrastive learning inherited the vocabulary: when we train with InfoNCE, we routinely say we are maximising a lower bound on $I(X;Y)$. If that bound were reliable, we could use the value of the loss as a measurement, compare representations by MI, and reason about information flow between layers. The 2019–2020 critiques say we cannot, and their reasons bear on what experiments count as evidence and what claims about "information" carry weight.

## The Donsker–Varadhan identity

Let $P$ and $Q$ be distributions on the same space with $P \ll Q$. The Donsker–Varadhan representation writes KL divergence as

$$ D_{KL}(P\|Q) = \sup_{T:\;E_Q[e^T]<\infty} \Big\{ E_P[T] - \log E_Q[e^T] \Big\}. $$

For any admissible $T$, the right-hand side is a lower bound on $D_{KL}$, so one can take a supremum over any parametric family of test functions. Equality holds when $T^*(x) = \log(dP/dQ)(x) + C$: the optimum is the log-density ratio, up to an additive shift. The gap at any $T$ is $D_{KL}(P\|G_T)$, where $G_T$ is the Gibbs-tilted distribution with density proportional to $e^T$ relative to $Q$. The bound is always below the truth, never above, and tight only at the right critic.

For mutual information, use $I(X;Y) = D_{KL}(P_{XY}\|P_X P_Y)$. Pick a critic $T_\theta(x,y)$, draw $m$ joint pairs $(x_i, y_i)$ for the $E_P$ term, and build "product" pairs — most often by shuffling a batch — for the $E_Q$ term:

$$ \hat I_{\text{MINE}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{m}\sum_i T_\theta(x_i, y_i) - \log \frac{1}{m}\sum_j e^{T_\theta(x_j^{\text{indep}}, y_j^{\text{indep}})}. $$

The first term is unbiased. The second is where everything goes wrong.

## The variance pathology

The partition function $E_Q[e^T]$ at the optimum equals $E_Q[e^{T^*}]$, which can be arbitrarily large when the density ratio is skewed. The empirical version $\frac{1}{m}\sum_j e^{T_\theta}$ is a Monte-Carlo estimate of an expectation of an exponential; its variance scales with $E_Q[e^{2T}] - (E_Q[e^T])^2$, and under the Gibbs optimum this quantity grows with the KL being estimated. A tighter critic — one closer to the log-density ratio — makes the first term of the estimator closer to its target and the second term wilder.

The clean statement, from Song and Ermon's 2020 analysis of these estimators, is that the sample variance of MINE-style estimators grows at least exponentially in the true mutual information. Informally, to resolve a mutual information of $I$ nats to a fixed relative accuracy with a DV-style estimator, the sample size has to scale like $e^I$. For $I = 10$ nats — modest, by the standards of a high-dimensional representation — that is twenty-two thousand samples minimum, under the most favourable conditions. Song and Ermon also show that popular estimators fail basic self-consistency properties of mutual information, such as data processing and additivity under independence, which is a bluntly non-mathematical way of saying that the numbers they report are not really measuring the thing they claim to.

The same intuition underlies McAllester and Stratos's 2020 formal limit. They prove that, without distributional assumptions, any high-confidence lower bound on $I$ computed from $N$ i.i.d. samples cannot exceed roughly $\log N$ nats. The ceiling is information-theoretic, not estimator-specific: imagine you had the best variational estimator conceivable, and it would still crash through the ceiling once the true MI exceeded $\log N$. Their recommendation, almost sheepish, is to estimate MI as a difference of entropies, each estimated via the cross-entropy of a conditional model, and accept that neither an upper nor a lower bound is guaranteed; at least the estimator converges at a $1/\sqrt N$ rate, which the variational ones do not.

Belghazi et al. partly anticipated the bias in their original paper. They used an exponential moving average to track the partition function during training, replacing the batch estimate by a smoothed version that is treated as a constant when computing gradients. For small learning rates, this gives an essentially unbiased gradient estimate. It is the right thing to do if you are using MINE as a loss. It does nothing for the variance of the estimator value, which is what matters when the number is being reported.

## The NWJ and InfoNCE siblings

Two alternatives keep showing up and are worth contrasting. The Nguyen–Wainwright–Jordan bound, which falls out of the convex-conjugate duality of $f$-divergences, writes

$$ I(X;Y) \ge E_{P_{XY}}[m(X,Y)] - e^{-1}\, E_{P_X P_Y}\big[e^{m(X,Y)}\big], $$

supremum over critics $m$. It is unbiased for a fixed critic — no logarithm of a sample mean, so no Jensen gap — and looser than DV. The exponential moment is still there, and the variance pathology with it.

InfoNCE, from the contrastive side, is both cleaner and more constrained. For $K$ pairs $(x_i, y_i)$ drawn from the joint and a critic $f$,

$$ \hat I_{\text{NCE}}(f;K) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^K \log \frac{e^{f(x_i,y_i)}}{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^K e^{f(x_i,y_j)}} \;\le\; \log K. $$

The cap follows from writing the inner expression as a $K$-way softmax and bounding each log by $\log K$. This is a feature, not a bug: InfoNCE replaces the problematic exponential of a free critic with a softmax normalised over $K$ samples, and its variance is controlled — at the price of a hard ceiling. You cannot use InfoNCE to measure mutual information above $\log K$. For a batch of 256, that is about 5.5 nats; for 4096, 8.3 nats. The contrastive community's practical workhorse is a lower bound that saturates well below quantities people regularly describe as "high MI."

## A concrete anchor

Here is the pathology on a toy problem where the ground truth is known. Let $X, Y$ be jointly Gaussian with correlation $\rho$; then $I(X;Y) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\log(1-\rho^2)$. Vary $\rho$ and compare estimators at a fixed sample size.

```python
import numpy as np

def toy_sample(rho, n):
    x = np.random.randn(n)
    y = rho * x + np.sqrt(1 - rho**2) * np.random.randn(n)
    return x, y

def mine_dv(x, y, critic):
    joint = critic(x, y)
    marg  = critic(x, np.random.permutation(y))
    return joint.mean() - np.log(np.exp(marg).mean())

def info_nce(x, y, critic):
    S = critic(x[:, None], y[None, :])        # K x K scores
    return (np.diag(S) - np.log(np.exp(S).mean(axis=1))).mean()

def mi_true(rho): return -0.5 * np.log(1 - rho**2)
```

Train a small MLP critic separately for $\rho \in \{0.5, 0.9, 0.99\}$, with true MI of 0.14, 0.83 and 1.96 nats. At $\rho = 0.5$ a DV-style estimator is within a few percent of the truth and run-to-run variance is small. At $\rho = 0.99$ the variance of the partition term dwarfs the mean: repeated runs with different seeds give answers that differ by more than their reported standard errors. An InfoNCE estimator with $K = 64$ caps at $\log 64 \approx 4.16$ nats and, at $\rho$ close to one, cannot in principle resolve differences above its cap even with an oracle critic. The failure is not a bug and it does not go away with a better network.

## What it implies in practice

A few consequences the practitioner has to carry around. If you are using MINE as a training signal, the gradient is still informative when the estimator value is not; the moving-average trick is designed for exactly this regime. But do not report the loss as an estimate of information in nats unless your mutual information is small relative to $\log$ (sample size). If you want to compare two representations by mutual information, prefer a bounded-class estimator — InfoNCE at a fixed $K$, or the cross-entropy-of-conditional-model recipe of McAllester and Stratos — over a free-critic DV estimator; you are trading a biased ceiling for an unreported variance disaster. And if your argument rests on "we have a lot of information between $X$ and $Y$," ask what evidence other than the estimator itself supports that, because the estimator alone cannot distinguish five nats from twenty.

Tschannen et al.'s 2020 paper takes this further. They train representations with tighter and looser MI bounds and show that tighter bounds often yield worse downstream performance. If maximising a tighter bound gives a worse representation, the thing being learned is not information in the mathematical sense; it is whatever side-effect the critic architecture and the sampling scheme pick out. This is not damning — it just says the explanation has to come from elsewhere.

## Limits and open questions

The $\log N$ ceiling is distribution-free; with parametric assumptions one can beat it, which is why the Kraskov–Stögbauer–Grassberger $k$-nearest-neighbour estimator sometimes outperforms neural estimators in low-dimensional settings. Song and Ermon's variance bounds are proved for specific critic classes; whether they extend to the fully nonparametric supremum is open. The InfoNCE cap can be pushed with larger $K$, mixture critics, decomposed estimators (DEMI, FlatNCE) and hybrids, but each moves the frontier by a few nats rather than qualitatively changing the regime.

More generally, the status of mutual information as an organising principle for self-supervised learning is unsettled. The critiques do not say the quantity is wrong. They say the measurement is unreliable in the regime where the quantity is interesting, and that the empirical success of "MI-maximising" methods owes as much to inductive bias in the critic and the sampling as to the quantity they nominally maximise. Treat the DV identity as a beautiful duality that happens to be hard to sample from, not as a drop-in measurement tool.

## Further reading

- Mohamed Ishmael Belghazi et al. *MINE: Mutual Information Neural Estimation.* ICML 2018. <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/belghazi18a.html>. The paper that pointed the DV identity at deep learning; the moving-average trick and the information-bottleneck experiments are what has aged best.
- Jiaming Song and Stefano Ermon. *Understanding the Limitations of Variational Mutual Information Estimators.* ICLR 2020. <https://iclr.cc/virtual_2020/poster_B1x62TNtDS.html>. The sharpest statement of the exponential-variance problem, with the SMILE clipping estimator and self-consistency diagnostics.
- David McAllester and Karl Stratos. *Formal Limitations on the Measurement of Mutual Information.* AISTATS 2020. <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v108/mcallester20a.html>. The $\log N$ ceiling as a theorem, plus the sober cross-entropy alternative.
- Ben Poole, Sherjil Ozair, Aaron van den Oord, Alexander Alemi, George Tucker. *On Variational Bounds of Mutual Information.* ICML 2019. <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/poole19a.html>. The unifying view: DV, NWJ, and InfoNCE as points on one continuum of bias-variance tradeoffs, with the interpolated bound.
- Michael Tschannen, Josip Djolonga, Paul K. Rubenstein, Sylvain Gelly, Mario Lucic. *On Mutual Information Maximization for Representation Learning.* ICLR 2020. <https://research.google/pubs/on-mutual-information-maximization-for-representation-learning/>. Tighter MI bounds, worse representations; the empirical argument that the MI framing is partly post-hoc.
- Weihao Gao, Sewoong Oh, Pramod Viswanath. *Demystifying Fixed k-Nearest Neighbor Information Estimators.* arXiv:1604.03006, 2016. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.03006>. The consistency proof for KSG and the BI-KSG refinement; the right reference when the nonparametric estimator is the honest choice.
